card.thesis: After inflation, the yearly cap on personal retirement account contributions is barely higher than when every worker first became eligible, and it covers fewer hours of typical pay.
card.overturns: "Retirement account contribution limits keep rising, so today's savers can shelter far more than earlier generations."

claim: The individual retirement account (IRA) contribution limit was set at $2,000 for tax years beginning in 1982, when IRAs opened to all workers, and stayed there until 2001, losing 45.5% of its purchasing power over that freeze. The 2026 limit is $7,500. In August-2026 dollars the 1982 limit was worth $6942.59, so after 44 years the cap is only 8.03% higher in real terms. Measured against the average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory workers, the 1982 cap equalled 254.3 hours of pay and the 2026 cap equals 230.6 hours (-9.32%): relative to pay, a saver can shelter less today than in 1982.

provisions.cite: 26 U.S.C. 219, Effective Date of 1981 Amendment note
provisions.quote: shall apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1981.
The limit on annual contributions to an IRA is increased to $7,500 from $7,000.

assumptions: Background (not recomputed): the 1981 amendments effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1981 also removed the bar on IRA deductions for workers covered by a workplace plan, which is why 1982 is described as the year every worker became eligible.

The IRA limit was $2,000 for every tax year 1982-2001 (the 2001 law replaced "$2,000" with "the deductible amount" starting 2002) and is $7,500 in 2026; catch-up contributions for age 50+ are ignored.
Price level for 1982 and 2001 = calendar-year mean of monthly CPI-U (NSA); price level for 2026 = August 2026 CPI-U, the latest observation.
Pay = average hourly earnings of production and nonsupervisory workers (a typical-worker wage), 1982 annual mean vs August 2026.
limits: History, not a forecast. The comparison is about the cap, not about what savers actually contribute; most savers contribute less than the cap. Workplace plans have separate, higher limits not covered here. The hourly-pay measure covers production and nonsupervisory workers only.
